title: Does Exercise Help a Hangover? Sweating It Out, Saunas & Cold Showers
excerpt: Can you sweat out a hangover? What exercise, saunas, and cold showers really do the morning after drinking, which workouts are safe, and when to stop and see a doctor.
metaDescription: Does exercise help a hangover? Why you can't sweat out alcohol, which workouts are safe the morning after, and why saunas and ice baths carry real risks.
author: DHM Guide Team
content:
**The honest answer first:** exercise does not cure a hangover, and you can't "sweat out" alcohol. Your liver clears more than 90% of the alcohol you drink, at a fairly steady pace, and only a small fraction leaves through sweat, breath, and urine. A workout won't speed that up in any way that matters. What gentle movement *can* do is make you feel a bit more awake and in a better mood once you've rehydrated and eaten. Hard workouts, hot saunas, and very cold plunges carry real risks the morning after, mostly because you're likely short on fluids and your heart and blood pressure are already under some strain.

**The quick rules:** Drink water and eat something before you move. If you still feel drunk, skip exercise entirely. If you feel okay, keep it light: a walk, an easy bike ride, gentle yoga, or a relaxed swim in a supervised pool. Leave the hot yoga, long runs, heavy lifting, and saunas for another day. A cool (not icy) shower is fine if it helps you wake up.

> **When to see a doctor.** This article is general information, not medical advice. **Stop exercising and get medical help if** you have chest pain, a racing or irregular heartbeat that doesn't settle with rest, fainting or near-fainting, severe shortness of breath, confusion, or vomiting so often that you can't keep fluids down. **Dark brown or cola-colored urine** with severe muscle pain or weakness after a workout can be a sign of muscle breakdown (rhabdomyolysis) and needs urgent care. If someone was drinking heavily and is very hard to wake, breathing slowly, or seizing, call 911. That's alcohol poisoning, not a hangover. And if you drink heavily most days and get shaking, sweating, anxiety, or a racing heart when you stop, those can be withdrawal symptoms rather than a hangover. Talk to a doctor before stopping or "sweating it out," because withdrawal can be dangerous.

## Can You Sweat Out Alcohol? The Short Science

This is the belief behind most hangover workouts, saunas, and hot yoga sessions, so it's worth getting right.

When you drink, alcohol is absorbed into your blood and travels to your liver. There, enzymes break it down: first into **acetaldehyde**, a toxic compound, and then into acetate, which your body uses or turns into carbon dioxide and water. This liver route handles the overwhelming majority of the alcohol. Only a small share, usually quoted at under 10%, leaves your body unchanged through your breath, urine, and sweat. That small share is why breathalyzers and alcohol-detecting skin patches work at all, but it's nowhere near enough to make sweating a way to clear alcohol.

Your liver works at a roughly fixed rate. A common rule of thumb is about one standard drink per hour, though it varies a lot between people. Exercise does not meaningfully raise that rate. Sweating more doesn't send more alcohol out through your skin in any amount that changes how you feel. Research on exercise and alcohol elimination has generally found little or no useful effect on how fast blood alcohol falls.

There's a second problem. By the morning, much of the alcohol may already be gone, and a hangover is mostly about what the alcohol left behind. Researchers think hangovers come from a mix of things:

- **Leftover acetaldehyde and other by-products** of alcohol breakdown
- **An immune and inflammatory response**, which helps explain the aches, fatigue, and "flu-like" feeling
- **Poor sleep**, since alcohol breaks up the second half of the night
- **Fluid and electrolyte shifts** from alcohol's effect on your kidneys
- **Low blood sugar** in some people, and stomach irritation
- **Congeners**, the extra compounds in darker drinks like whiskey and red wine

Sweating doesn't fix any of those. If anything, losing more fluid works against you. For a fuller tour of what causes a hangover, see our [complete hangover science guide](/never-hungover/complete-hangover-science-hub-2025).

## Why You Might Feel Better After Exercise Anyway

Plenty of people swear a morning run "fixed" their hangover. They're not imagining the improvement, but the reasons are different from what they think.

- **Time is passing.** Hangovers ease as the hours go by. An hour of exercise is an hour your body spent recovering.
- **You probably drank water.** Most people drink something during or after a workout, and rehydrating helps headaches and fatigue.
- **Movement lifts mood and alertness.** Exercise reliably improves mood and energy in the short term, partly through stress hormones and brain chemicals like endorphins. That can take the edge off the low, foggy feeling.
- **Fresh air and daylight.** A walk outside can help reset a groggy brain and nudge your body clock after a late night.
- **Distraction.** Focusing on something other than how bad you feel genuinely helps how bad you feel.

So the honest version is: light exercise can help you *feel* better, and it's a perfectly reasonable thing to do once you're stable. There is no good evidence that it removes alcohol faster or treats the underlying causes of a hangover.

## The Risks of Working Out Hungover

The morning after drinking is not a normal training day. Several things stack against you.

### You're probably low on fluids

Alcohol suppresses a hormone called vasopressin (also called antidiuretic hormone), which normally tells your kidneys to hold on to water. With less of it around, you urinate more than you drink. Add sweating in a warm bar, possible vomiting, and a night without water, and many people start the day short on fluids and salts. Exercise, especially in heat, makes you lose more. That raises the risk of dizziness, cramps, headaches, and heat illness.

Interestingly, hangover researchers have found that how dehydrated people are doesn't line up neatly with how bad their hangover feels. So rehydrating won't cure a hangover on its own. But being short on fluids does make hard exercise less safe, which is the point that matters here.

### Your heart may be under strain

Heavy drinking can raise your resting heart rate the next day, and binge drinking is a known trigger for irregular heart rhythms, most often atrial fibrillation. Doctors sometimes call this "holiday heart" because it shows up after weekends and holidays. Pushing your heart rate high on top of that, while dehydrated, is not a good combination. If your heart feels like it's racing or fluttering at rest, that's a sign to skip the workout.

### Your coordination and judgment are off

Hangovers impair attention, reaction time, and coordination, even when you no longer feel drunk. After a very heavy night, you may still have alcohol in your blood the next morning. That matters for anything where a slip hurts: lifting heavy weights, cycling in traffic, trail running, climbing, or swimming in open water.

### Your performance will be worse

This one is less dangerous but worth knowing. Alcohol and poor sleep reduce endurance, strength, and power output the next day, and it will feel harder than usual. Alcohol also blunts muscle protein synthesis, the process your body uses to repair and build muscle after training. A small study in trained men (Parr and colleagues, published in *PLOS ONE* in 2014) found that drinking a large amount of alcohol after exercise reduced muscle protein synthesis even when protein was eaten alongside it. A hard session the morning after a big night may give you less benefit than usual. Our guide on [alcohol and muscle recovery](/never-hungover/alcohol-protein-synthesis-muscle-recovery-impact-guide-2025) goes deeper.

### Your blood sugar may be low

Alcohol interferes with the liver's ability to release sugar into the blood. Some people wake up with low blood sugar after drinking, especially if they didn't eat much. Exercising on an empty stomach in that state can bring on shakiness, weakness, and lightheadedness.

## Does a Hangover Workout Help? What Kind Is Okay

If you feel up to moving, the type and intensity matter far more than whether you exercise at all. Here's a practical guide for social drinkers the morning after.

| Activity | Hungover verdict | Why |
|---|---|---|
| Walking outdoors | Good choice | Low strain, daylight, fresh air, easy to stop |
| Easy cycling (stationary or quiet route) | Usually fine | Keep it conversational; avoid traffic if you're foggy |
| Gentle yoga or stretching | Usually fine | Helps stiffness; skip inversions if nauseous |
| Easy swim in a supervised pool | Okay if fully sober | Never swim alone or in open water after drinking |
| Moderate jog | Proceed with caution | Only if hydrated, fed, and feeling steady |
| Heavy lifting | Skip it | Coordination and grip are off; injury risk |
| HIIT, long runs, races | Skip it | High heart rate on top of dehydration and heart strain |
| Hot yoga or heated classes | Skip it | Adds heat stress and fluid loss to a fluid deficit |

A simple test: if you'd hesitate to drive, don't do anything more demanding than a walk. If you feel steady and you've had water and food, a light session is reasonable. Stop if you feel dizzy, sick, or your heart starts pounding.

### A simple hangover workout plan

If you want a structure, here's a sensible one:

1. **Rehydrate first.** Drink a large glass or two of water, ideally with some electrolytes, and wait 20 to 30 minutes.
2. **Eat something easy.** Toast, a banana, eggs, or oatmeal gives your body some fuel and helps steady blood sugar.
3. **Move gently for 20 to 40 minutes.** Walk, cycle easily, or stretch. Keep your effort at a level where you could hold a conversation.
4. **Keep drinking fluids** during and after.
5. **Rest afterward** rather than piling on a second session.

For more on fluids, see our guide to [whether electrolytes help before or after drinking](/never-hungover/electrolytes-before-or-after-drinking) and our roundup of the [best hangover recovery drinks](/never-hungover/best-hangover-recovery-drinks).

## Does a Sauna Help a Hangover?

This is one of the most searched versions of the "sweat it out" idea, and it's the one we'd most strongly discourage.

A sauna heats your body, widens your blood vessels, drops your blood pressure, raises your heart rate, and makes you sweat heavily. Those effects are part of why regular sauna use can be pleasant and relaxing for healthy, sober people. After drinking, they all point the wrong way:

- **More fluid loss** when you're already likely short on fluids
- **Lower blood pressure**, which alcohol also lowers, making fainting more likely, especially when you stand up
- **A higher heart rate**, on top of alcohol's strain on heart rhythm
- **Impaired judgment** about how long you've been in there and how you're feeling

This isn't theoretical. In Finland, where saunas are part of daily life, forensic research on sauna deaths has found that alcohol was involved in a large share of them. Finnish health guidance has long advised against using a sauna while drinking.

And as covered above, the sweat won't carry away the alcohol or the by-products that cause your hangover. You'll lose water and salt, not the hangover.

**Our verdict:** skip the sauna, steam room, and hot tub the morning after drinking, and absolutely skip them while you're still drinking. If you love the sauna, save it for a day when you're well hydrated and sober.

## Do Cold Showers Help a Hangover?

Cold water is the other half of the "shock it out" playbook. The honest picture here is milder than the sauna.

A cool or cold shower can make you feel more awake. Cold exposure triggers a quick rise in alertness hormones like noradrenaline, along with faster breathing and a jump in heart rate. Many people find that genuinely refreshing when they're groggy. There's no good evidence that it speeds up alcohol clearance or treats the causes of a hangover, but feeling more alert can make the morning more bearable.

The cautions:

- **Avoid ice baths and very cold plunges while hungover, and never while drunk.** Sudden immersion in very cold water causes a "cold shock" response: an involuntary gasp, rapid breathing, and a spike in heart rate and blood pressure. That's a heart strain you don't need after heavy drinking, and in open water, the gasp reflex is a drowning risk.
- **Alcohol interferes with temperature control.** It makes you feel warm while your body is actually losing heat. That's one reason cold water is especially risky after drinking.
- **A cool shower is the safe middle ground.** Start warm, then turn it cooler for the last 30 to 60 seconds if you want the wake-up effect.

For more on cold exposure and drinking, see our [cold therapy and alcohol recovery guide](/never-hungover/cold-therapy-alcohol-recovery-guide-2025).

## What Actually Helps a Hangover

If exercise, saunas, and cold plunges aren't the answer, what is? The evidence for any single hangover remedy is weak, and there is no good evidence that anything reliably cures one. But a few basics help most people feel better faster:

- **Water and electrolytes.** They won't cure a hangover on their own, but they ease dehydration headaches and help you feel more human. An oral rehydration drink is useful if you've been vomiting.
- **Food.** Easy carbohydrates help with low blood sugar, and a proper meal steadies your stomach. Eggs, toast, bananas, and broth-based soups are common choices.
- **Sleep or rest.** Alcohol wrecks sleep quality, so a nap or a slow morning often does more than anything else.
- **A pain reliever, used carefully.** Ibuprofen with food can help a headache. Be careful with acetaminophen (Tylenol) if you drink heavily; our [Tylenol and alcohol guide](/never-hungover/tylenol-and-alcohol) explains why.
- **Time.** Most hangovers fade within 24 hours.

For a full rundown of what has some evidence and what doesn't, read our [science-based guide to curing a hangover](/never-hungover/how-to-cure-a-hangover-complete-science-guide). And because the best hangover is the one you don't get, our guide on [how to prevent a hangover](/never-hungover/how-to-prevent-a-hangover) covers pacing, food, and drink choice.

## Exercising Before or While Drinking

A related question: can a workout *before* a night out reduce the hangover? There's no good evidence that it does. A hard session right before drinking can actually make things worse in a few ways. You may be dehydrated before your first drink, and if you've emptied your glycogen stores and skipped a meal, alcohol may hit you faster. Some people also feel the effects of alcohol more strongly after hard exercise.

If you train on the day you plan to drink, eat a proper meal afterward, rehydrate fully, and go easier on the drinks. Exercising while drinking, such as at a festival or a sports day, raises the risk of dehydration, heat illness, and injury, so keep water in the mix.

## Who Should Skip Exercise Entirely the Morning After

Be especially careful, and consider resting instead, if any of these apply:

- You still feel drunk or unsteady
- You vomited during the night or this morning
- You have a heart condition, high blood pressure, or a history of fainting
- You have diabetes, especially if you use insulin or medicines that can cause low blood sugar
- You take medicines that cause drowsiness or affect blood pressure
- It's hot outside, or the planned workout is long or intense
- You slept only a few hours

In those cases, rest, fluids, and food are the better plan. Your fitness won't suffer from one rest day.

## Where DHM Fits In

Some people who drink socially try supplements to help the morning after. **DHM (dihydromyricetin)** is a plant compound from the Japanese raisin tree that's been studied for its effects on alcohol metabolism and the liver. Most of the research is from animal and lab studies, with limited human data, so it's promising rather than proven. It won't make a hungover workout safe, and it isn't a substitute for water, food, sleep, and sensible drinking.

If you want to try DHM, a straightforward, good-value option is [Double Wood DHM](https://www.amazon.com/dp/B074N712FM?tag=dhmguide-20). Our [DHM dosage guide](/never-hungover/dhm-dosage-guide-2025) covers how much people typically take and when.

## The Bottom Line

- You can't sweat out alcohol. Your liver clears it at a steady pace, and exercise doesn't meaningfully speed that up.
- Light exercise, like a walk or gentle yoga, can help you feel more alert and in a better mood once you've had water and food.
- Skip hard workouts, heavy lifting, hot yoga, and long runs the morning after a big night. Dehydration, heart strain, and poor coordination make them riskier.
- Avoid saunas and hot tubs after drinking. They add fluid loss and low blood pressure to a body that already has both.
- A cool shower is fine for waking up. Skip ice baths and cold plunges while hungover, and never do them drunk.
- Chest pain, a racing or irregular heartbeat, fainting, confusion, or dark urine with severe muscle pain means stop and get medical help.

## Frequently Asked Questions

**Does exercise help a hangover?**

Light exercise can help you feel more alert and improve your mood, but it doesn't cure a hangover or clear alcohol faster. If you're hydrated, have eaten, and feel steady, a walk, easy bike ride, or gentle yoga is reasonable. Skip hard workouts the morning after heavy drinking, because dehydration, heart strain, and poor coordination make them riskier.

**Can you sweat out alcohol?**

No. Your liver breaks down more than 90% of the alcohol you drink, at a fairly steady rate of roughly one standard drink per hour. Only a small fraction leaves through sweat, breath, and urine, and exercising or sitting in a sauna doesn't change that in any meaningful way. Sweating mostly costs you water and salt.

**Does a sauna help a hangover?**

There is no good evidence that a sauna helps a hangover, and it can be risky. Saunas cause heavy sweating, lower blood pressure, and raise heart rate, all of which add to the strain alcohol has already put on your body. Forensic research from Finland has found alcohol involved in a large share of sauna deaths. Skip the sauna, steam room, and hot tub after drinking.

**Do cold showers help a hangover?**

A cool shower can make you feel more awake, which may make the morning easier, but there is no good evidence that it treats a hangover or speeds up alcohol clearance. Avoid ice baths and cold plunges while hungover, and never while drunk, because sudden cold immersion causes a gasp reflex and a spike in heart rate and blood pressure.

**Is it bad to work out hungover?**

A light workout is usually fine if you feel steady and have had water and food. Intense exercise is a bad idea, because you're likely short on fluids, your heart rate may already be raised, your coordination is off, and your performance will be worse. Stop if you feel dizzy, sick, or your heart starts pounding or fluttering.

**What is the best hangover workout?**

A 20- to 40-minute walk outdoors is hard to beat. Easy cycling, gentle yoga, and stretching are also good options. Drink water and eat something first, keep the effort at a level where you can hold a conversation, and keep sipping fluids afterward. Save heavy lifting, intervals, and long runs for another day.

**Should I exercise before drinking to avoid a hangover?**

There's no good evidence that exercising before drinking prevents a hangover. A hard workout right before a night out can leave you dehydrated and low on fuel, which may make alcohol hit harder. If you train on a drinking day, eat a proper meal, rehydrate, and pace your drinks.

**When should I see a doctor after exercising hungover?**

Get medical help for chest pain, a racing or irregular heartbeat that doesn't settle with rest, fainting, severe shortness of breath, confusion, or vomiting that stops you keeping fluids down. Dark brown or cola-colored urine with severe muscle pain or weakness can signal muscle breakdown and needs urgent care.
